title: Setting up electric fencing for pigs
subtitle: Why pigs respect electric fencing and how to set up a basic paddock system.
excerpt: Pigs learn to respect electric fencing quickly once they have been trained to it. A single strand at snout height is enough to contain most pigs on open ground. A permanent outer fence plus portable electric inner fencing allows paddock rotation without rebuilding full post-and-rail sections. Here is the setup sequence.
sourceNotes: BPEX, pig welfare housing and outdoor management (2015). NFU, electric fencing for pigs guidance. John Seymour, Self-Sufficient Life (2009), pig management chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: A device that delivers a short, high-voltage pulse through an electric fence at regular intervals (typically once per second). Mains-powered energisers suit permanent installations; battery or solar energisers suit portable paddock systems.

The initial process of introducing pigs to an electric fence in a controlled environment so they learn the association between the wire and the shock before relying on the fence for containment. Pigs trained correctly are very reliable to contain.

content.text: more reliably than cattle or sheep because their sensitive snouts contact the wire at snout height before any other part of their body. One good shock from a correctly energised fence is usually enough for a pig to avoid the wire for weeks. Unlike sheep, pigs do not push through fencing out of panic or flock pressure.
Energiser: minimum 0.5 joule output for a small paddock. A 1 to 2 joule energiser handles most small-holding pig systems and gives a detectable shock through thick winter mud.
Wire or polytape: first strand at 20 to 30 cm (snout height for weaners). Add a second strand at 50 to 60 cm for large adults or sows with piglets.
Posts: step-in plastic posts at 5 to 8 m intervals are adequate for portable paddocks on level ground.
An outer permanent fence (pig-wire or post-and-rail) as a backup. Do not rely solely on electric fencing as the outer boundary of a holding where pigs could access a road or neighbour's land.

should happen in a small, solid-fenced pen before the electric fence becomes the primary boundary. Set up a single strand inside the solid pen. Bait the wire with something the pigs will investigate, such as a smear of peanut butter or a piece of bread. Let them touch the wire and receive a shock. Most pigs then avoid the wire for days without further persuasion. After two to three days, the solid outer fence can be removed.
Check the voltage on the fence with a fence tester each morning. Below 2000V on a wet day or 3000V on a dry day suggests a fault: vegetation touching the wire is the most common cause.
Walk the fence line and remove any grass, brambles, or nettles touching the wire. These drain current to earth and reduce the shock.
Check the earth stake. The energiser ground rod should be driven at least 50 cm into moist soil. In dry summers, water around the ground rod to maintain contact.
